The Rotunda Circle · Test Figure — From a Real Statue

Zeus, son of Cronus and Rhea, king of Olympus: god of the sky and the storm, whose weapon is the thunderbolt and whose word the other gods obey. His bird is the eagle, who carries the bolt in a hundred ancient images; his tree is the oak, and at Dodona his oracle spoke through oak leaves. The head follows the classical types — the marble Zeus of Otricoli and the great bronze found in the sea off Cape Artemision, cast around 460 BCE. Scholars still argue over that bronze: if the lost weapon was a thunderbolt he is Zeus; if a trident, Poseidon. The hand is empty, and the argument has never closed.

This figure is not modelled by hand — it is a true 3D scan of that bronze. The original, over life size and cast around 460–450 BCE, was raised from the sea off Cape Artemision and stands today in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. The scan was made by SMK — the National Gallery of Denmark — from the full-size plaster cast (KAS2100) in its Royal Cast Collection in Copenhagen, and released into the public domain (CC0 1.0); the Archives prepared the mesh for the web, slimming the body for phones while keeping the head and face at the scan’s full strength. On screen the figure wears bronze, the metal of the Athens original, where the scanned cast is plaster — one single dark bronze over the whole figure, body and drape alike, as a cast statue is finished; that finish is ours, and we say so plainly. And the old question stands in the figure itself: the raised hand is empty. Bolt or trident, Zeus or Poseidon — the sea kept the weapon, and the argument with it. In these halls the figure is presented draped, as the museum keeps its rooms open to every age.
